a neural signature that can help to predict whether individuals with depression are likely

I know currently doctors often use trial and error to find the best antidepressant for a

So let's go more into the details of those sophisticated data analytic methods.

this current research. So earlier research suggested that specific
components of brain activity as measured by resting state electroencephalography

We use this insight along with insights from other fields such as neuroscience, clinical

We use the algorithm to analyze data from participants in a large clinical trial of the

predicted participants' depressive symptoms after treatment.
Okay, just to make sure I understand. So you knew there was a way of analyzing brain

Well, I wouldn't say we knew, but that was our hypothesis.
Yes, of course. So, what were the results of the study?

Hello everyone. Today I'm here to talk about a very simple and low-cost way of reducing
the risk of further tooth decay in young children by more than a quarter. Yes, by more than
a quarter. So first, let me back up a bit and tell you about the statistics that prompted
this research, as well as the research that helped us come to this finding.
First of all, nearly a quarter of all five-year-olds in the United Kingdom experienced tooth decay.
In particular, children from the most deprived areas are more than twice the level of decay
than those from the least-deprived.
Another statistic that some of you may not be aware of is that tooth decay is the single
highest reason for children to be admitted to hospital, but nearly 34,000 children aged
nine or under admitted to hospitals have teeth extracted in the last year.
In addition to causing pain, sleepless nights and days of missed school and work for children
and their families, each extraction costs the NHS around £1,000 and normally needs to be
done under general anaesthetic.
We can certainly say that this is an unpleasant experience for all involved and a completely
avoidable expense.
In addition, evidence shows that children who have baby teeth taken out are much more likely
to get decay again in their adult teeth.
research in this area suggests that parents often know what has caused the tooth decay
in their young children but find it very difficult to change habits so they find it
hard to know where to start.
So the trial that led us to the finding I mentioned at the beginning of my presentation
took place in 12 centres in the United Kingdom and involved over 200 families of 5-7 year
old children having baby teeth extracted in hospital.
In order to tackle the problem of tooth decay and difficult to change habits, my research
team developed a talking intervention for trained dental nurses to have conversations
with parents of children who were having teeth extracted. The conversations with dental nurses
focused on how families could prevent tooth decay in the future and on how to choose goals
that they felt they could achieve.
To give you an idea of how this approach was different from what is normally done, here
is what one of the nurses involved in the study had to say. She said that she finds that if
we give lots of information guidance all at once it can be overwhelming for parents.
In this trial we help families choose one or two actions. For example, it might be to
help brush their children's teeth at night or stop giving a sugary snack at bedtime. It
became the parents' goal, not ours, and so they could see a way forward and they took
ownership of the situation. Two years later we compared outcomes for these
children with those who had been given standard advice after regular visits to
the dentist and we also asked the children's dentists about care
provided. We found that nearly two-thirds of children in both groups went back to
the dentist. However, the children whose families had not spoken to the
specially trained dental nurses needed many more fillings. Children whose
families had set their own dental health goals, had significantly healthier teeth, and had
a 29% lower risk of having new tooth decay.
Our main conclusion from this research is that when we change how we talk to parents
about prevention, their children go on to develop fewer cavities. The key is helping
parents to choose one or two behaviours they feel they can change for their child, rather
than us telling parents what to do, and that makes the difference. So it turns out that
a simple and cost-effective method to reduce tooth decay in small children is a conversation,
one that seeks to create a partnership between parents and dental service providers. I think
we can also all agree that this is much more pleasant for all involved, and the habits
established by the children involved in this study will likely have a positive effect on
all areas of their health. We are currently in the process of developing our work into
a training module for dental nurses in the NHS and hope to make it available in the next
couple of months.
